The contribution of this paper includes:
* The paper proposes an interesting setting for programming language transpilation, specifically between deep learning frameworks (e.g. PyTorch, Keras and MXNet);

* A comprehensive corpus of PyTorch-Keras-MXNet source code is constructed. Also a benchmark to evaluate the transpilation is established for future research.

content.title: Response to Reviewer SPxn
content.comment:
Thank you for your helpful comments. We respond to your comments below to address your concerns.

### Weakness 1

> The idea of using NN-based methods for transpilation is not well motivated. Deterministic and correctness-guaranteed transpilation widely exists in DL compilers, for example, Torch-XLA, TVM-Torch/TensorFlow/MXNet/Torch, and usually does not require extensive engineering (couple of thousands lines of code).

The “deterministic and correctness-guaranteed transpilation” methods mentioned by the reviewer are all **rule-based** that match on code patterns and they all require extensive engineering and are error-prone. For example, Torch-XLA consists of transpilation rules of all PyTorch operators, resulting in 44,873 lines of C++ codes and and 24,081 lines of Python codes, from 3,133 Git commits. As is discussed in our paper, such rule-based methods are not scalable and hard to maintain. We are unaware of any prior work that is able to perform such transpilation using non rule-based methods, and ours is a first step towards transpiling DL codes **without devising code-matching rules** .

Also, the task we address in this work is source-to-source *transpilation* between code written using different deep learning frameworks; we are not building *DL compilers* . In *transpilation* , both the input and the output should be deep-learning source codes, preferably readable by humans. The source code and the target code are at the same level of abstraction. However, the examples given in this review, such as Torch-XLA and TVM, focus on *compiling* deep learning source codes to intermediate representations (IR) using standard pattern matching-driven compilation, with the compiled code to be executed using domain-specific hardware, such as TPUs and GPUs. In this case, the target is usually in a lower level of abstraction, and the generated code is not designed to be readable by humans.


### Weakness 2

> No direct metric is clearly established to reflect the effectiveness of the domain-specific task. In Section 3, EM, F1, BLEU and edit distance are listed as metrics, but as a transpilation task, the directly correctness-related metrics, for example, structural equality of the IR being translated, is not proper part of discussion, which could cast some doubt on the reliability of transpilation.

The *exact match (EM)* metric we are using requires a transpiled program to be exactly the same as the ground truth after canonicalization. It is even **more strict than the IR equivalence** metric mentioned in the review. We do not use IR equivalence because the task we are addressing is *transpiling* instead of lowering source code to an intermediate representation. For example, if a correct program is syntactically obfuscated, it would still be deemed as correct based on IR equivalence, but that is not what we want as such obfuscated programs lack human readability.

content.title: Thank you for your response!
content.comment:
Thank you for sharing your perspective! It is definitely valuable to us.

The contribution I appreciated the most is the dataset and the task setting per se, as it assists cross-framework transpilation automatically by leveraging web crawl non-parallel data, which would make a huge impact if it is developed as an assistant tool for researchers/engineers to productionalize deep learning code.

As a long-time practitioner in machine learning compilers and python-embedded DSLs, I would love to further dissect and clarify my perspective.

> Torch-XLA consists of transpilation rules of all PyTorch operators, resulting in 44,873 lines of C++ codes and and 24,081 lines of Python codes, from 3,133 Git commits

- MXNet-to-TVM and Torch-to-TVM are 2,932 and 4,655 lines of python code, respectively, located under `python/tvm/relay/frontend`.
- Translation in torch-xla locates under `torch_xla/csrc/ops`, which, despite much syntactic noise, is 10,667 lines of C++ code;

Meanwhile, the clarification above does not undermine the primary contribution of this paper in any sense, because the paper instead focuses on a purely automatic setting of transpilation without human intervention, but in terms of writing, there would be more accurate if we would adopt a slightly different perspective: rule-based method per se is not inherently bad or challenging in transpilation specifically for deep learning models.

> The exact match (EM) metric we are using requires a transpiled program to be exactly the same as the ground truth after canonicalization. It is even more strict than the IR equivalence metric mentioned in the review.

Indeed exact match is a long-tested metric in machine translation, which undoubtedly is helpful for reviewers to understand how well a proposed approach works. However, as I personally view the primary contribution of this paper as the establishment of the dataset and the unsupervised task per se, a task-specific metric would provide more insights under the hood of the proposed and follow-up approaches. To share some examples that EM will likely not be the best fit:
- One-to-many mapping: an operator, say `reshape` could be translated across frameworks directly, or slightly tweaked into `flatten` or other operators.
- Repetitive patterns: for example, a tensor could be repetitively reshaped without affecting semantical correctness, a -> reshape([10, 20]) -> reshape([200]) -> reshape([10, 20]). While EM doesn't acknowledge that they could be identical, the transpilation, by definition, could be correct but just less effective.
- Direct translation: many operators across different frameworks share exactly the same meaning, for example, sin, ReLU. In those cases, EM could give a really high score but fails to focus on the part where translation might go wrong comparably easily.
- Side effects and control flow equivalence: those are the real challenging tasks in transpilation, but they are not quite a focus with EM metric.

Overall, it is nice work with clear contribution. The reviewer believes the topic could potentially be more interesting if more task-specific insights are provided.

replying_to: Replying to Thank you for your response!

content.title: Thank you for your comments
content.comment:
Thank you for sharing your valuable ideas from the perspective of ML compilers. We respond to each of your comments below:

### About weakness 1

Thank you for your clarification of the complexity of DL compilers and acknowledging our contribution to building a purely automatic transpiler without human intervention. We will reword relevant claims about rule-based compilers/transpilers in the introduction section according to your comments.

### About weakness 2

IR equivalence, or semantic/computational equivalence, has many advantages as mentioned in your comment. However, evaluating IR equivalence is difficult, and unnecessary for source-to-source transpilation between DL frameworks.

Computing IR equivalence is **difficult**. Semantic equivalence for general programs is undecidable, and we are unaware of solvers that can decide such equivalence even for DL programs. An approximation to semantic equivalence can be computed by feeding examples into the program and comparing the outputs. However, as our training and evaluation data is crawled from the web, we do not have the data required to generate valid inputs (e.g., input tensor shapes, types, and value ranges). Most codes also require high-powered GPUs to be executed.

Computing IR equivalence is also **unnecessary** for evaluating transpilation systems mentioned in this paper. The important baselines mentioned in this paper are the big LMs, GPT-3, and Codex. The prototypical errors in using them for transpilation are (1) calling nonexistent API functions (e.g., `layers.Linear` in Keras); (2) wrong argument orderings (e.g., the multi-head attention example in Table 2); and (3) irrelevant extra code lines (see Table 2). For each type of error, IR equivalence and EM would give the same result (i.e., both would return 0). Therefore, the claims we made in this paper still hold even if we use the EM score as the metric.

We do agree that IR equivalence is a better metric for most transpilation/compilation tasks, but for the evaluation of systems mentioned in this paper, we believe that the exact match metric is accurate enough.

> The reviewer believes the topic could potentially be more interesting if more task-specific insights are provided.

The key contribution of ADELT is that we **decouple** the transpilation of the code skeleton and the mapping of API keywords. **This technique is motivated by the task-specific insight** that code skeletons of DL programs are easy to transpile using big LMs, since in DL programs, code skeletons are usually highly homogeneous Python boilerplate codes, while the API keywords are more difficult to transpile. Based on this insight, we train a separate model to learn API keyword mappings using an in-domain program corpus.

That said, we noticed that well-known LMs, even those trained on code such as Codex, perform poorly on the transpilation of DL programs out of the box. We believe that is due to LMs inability to understand the meaning of functions that are embedded within boilerplate codes. As such, we design the hierarchical dictionary generation algorithm (Section 2.4) specifically for transpiling DL programs. By leveraging the structure of function definitions, our hierarchical dictionary generation algorithm improves the accuracy and guarantees that argument mappings are consistent with function mappings in the generated dictionary. Our results show that this works particularly well for DL programs as functions in this domain tend to correspond in a one-to-one manner across different DL frameworks.

content.title: Response to Reviewer B7Ti
content.comment:
Thank you for your helpful comments. We did some further explorations after we submitted the original version, and we revise the paper according to your comments. The most important change in the new version is that ADELT can now be integrated with a pretrained big LM that does skeletal code transpilation. This change removes the limitation of ADELT to keyword transpilation, making it more flexible and generalizable. We respond to your comments below to address your concerns.

### Weakness 1

> The evaluation only considers the domain of DL libraries (which seems to be relatively simple), while there could be more scenarios where code-translation would be helpful.

ADELT is indeed specific to DL code transpilation, but we argue that the task of transpilation between DL frameworks is interesting, important, and also challenging. As we mentioned in the Introduction, with new DL frameworks appearing every year, migrating deep learning codes from one framework to another has become a tedious chore for most DL practitioners. An automated tool will help developers overcome this difficulty. Simply applying existing methods in NL/Code translation to this task does not work very well as we have discovered, and we address the challenges arising from DL code transpilation using techniques such as canonicalization, hierarchical generation, and decoupling code skeleton with keywords. Even though we only illustrate using DL code transpilation, we believe some of our techniques should be generalized to other tasks as well, such as transpilation between different SQL dialects, or even data visualization APIs.

### Weakness 2

> The framework is mostly based on simple keyword translation (with some slight explorations on one-to-many cases), while there could be more complex scenarios of code transpilation which only changing keywords is not enough. It might be reasonable to at least add more discussions on this.

Most cases in the transpilation between deep learning frameworks are one-one API keyword mappings because DL frameworks usually follow similar designs. There are cases where such mappings are not one-one mappings, and we show in Section 3.6 and Appendix A.9. Our model can also solve such cases if enough unlabeled training data is available. **In our updated version of the paper, we have improved ADELT such that the entire transpilation is fully automated, using a pretrained big language model to transpile the code skeleton**. This makes ADELT more flexible and generalizable to cases beyond API keyword substitutions.

By the way, I also suggest focusing more on the exact match metric since this would be the one that is more meaningful in this application than metrics like BLEU. I think I will tend to keep my original score unchanged.

content.title: Thank you for your comments
content.comment: Thank you for your suggestion of focusing on the exact match metric. The exact match score is already the default metric that we refer to in discussion and analysis throughout this paper. In transpiling between deep learning frameworks, we were unable to find complex one-to-many mappings as all the ones we are aware of are one-to-one. That said, to investigate this further, we created a synthetic dataset where there are more one-to-many API mappings as discussed in Appendix A.9. Using that dataset, we trained a new model, ADELT+, and our evaluation shows that it is capable of modeling one-to-many mappings when enough unlabeled training data is available. We would love to try out more complex real-word cases that the reviewer is aware of.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper focuses on unsupervised code translation between different deep learning frameworks, including PyTorch-MXNet and PyTorch-Keras, and designs a simple pipeline named ADELT for this task. The whole method is based on API calls and learns the API keyword translation dictionary in an unsupervised way, which is used to replace each keyword with its translation during code translation.  The authors build the DL Corpus for automatic evaluation. Experiments on the DL Corpus show that ADELT obtains better performance than other simple unsupervised methods and few-shot adaptation of pre-trained language models (e.g., GPT-3 and Codex).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- This paper designs a new pipeline named ADELT for unsupervised code translation between different deep learning frameworks.
- This paper constructs a useful dataset, DL corpus, which may benefit other researchers and the community.

Weaknesses:
- The main core of the proposed framework is unsupervised "word" translation. Domain-adversarial training has been explored in unsupervised word translation tasks. The technical contribution of this paper is limited.
- The code translation between different DL frameworks seems easy since the proposed ADELT introduces some tricks for this task, including canonicalization and translating API keywords only. The proposed method may not be well generalised to other code translation tasks (e.g., between different program languages).
- The method comparisons are only based on the sentence-level evaluation. I am unsure of the effectiveness of this method on true settings, e.g., generating a TensorFlow/MXNet version of the Pytorch-based DL models or toolkits.

Detailed Comments:

Overall, this paper is easy to follow and this idea is straightforward. The proposed code translation pipeline between different DL frameworks makes sense and the constructed dataset is useful. My main concern is the extension of this proposed method. As ADELT introduces some tricks for this task, including canonicalization and translating API keywords only, this code translation between different DL frameworks seems easy and oversimplification in my view.  Thus, I doubt that the proposed method could be well generalised to other code translation tasks (e.g., between different program languages).

In addition,  the main technical contribution of the proposed framework is domain-adversarial training for unsupervised "word" translation that is limited to API keywords. Since domain-adversarial training has been explored in unsupervised word translation tasks, the novelty of the proposed method is limited. Instead of sentence-level evaluation, I am very interested to observe the effectiveness of this method on true settings, e.g., generating a TensorFlow/MXNet version of the Pytorch-based models or DL toolkits and then training models with this version.


Questions for the Author(s):
- What if the API keywords are not aligned well in different DL frameworks? It seems that the proposed method would fail in this situation.
- For the construction of the API keyword translation dictionary, do you try to leverage the technical document of API calls to directly align the API keyword in different DL frameworks? I think it is an easy way to achieve this goal.
- Please provides some example comparisons of model modules.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper investigates unsupervised code translation between different DL frameworks, including PyTorch-MXNet and PyTorch-Keras, and designs a simple and effective pipeline for this task. This code translation task seems oversimplification in my view, due to canonicalization and translating API keywords only. The proposed method may not be well generalised to other code translation tasks (e.g., between different program languages). The technical contribution of this paper is also limited.

content.title: Response to Reviewer rE5P (Part 1)
content.comment:
Thank you for your helpful comments.  According to your comments, we updated the paper and added Appendix A.10, in which we added two extra examples, and Appendix A.11, where describe how ADELT can be applied to transpilation tasks across different PLs. We respond to your comments below to address your concerns.

### Weakness 1

> The main core of the proposed framework is unsupervised "word" translation. Domain-adversarial training has been explored in unsupervised word translation tasks. The technical contribution of this paper is limited.

To our best knowledge, ADELT is the first work that applies domain-adversarial methods used in natural language word translation to transpilation of programming languages (PLs). Moreover, our technical contribution lies further than simply applying domain-adversarial methods to another domain. Specifically, we **tackle the  challenges specific to programming languages** transpilation by designing a code canonicalization and keyword extraction pipeline. We also **leverage properties specific to PL** , such as the hierarchical structure of API calls (each API call consists of one API function reference plus multiple parameters), and design a hierarchical dictionary generation algorithm for APIs. Moreover, in the new version, we also **integrate word translation techniques with pretrained big language models** .

### Weakness 2

> The code translation between different DL frameworks seems easy since the proposed ADELT introduces some tricks for this task, including canonicalization and translating API keywords only. The proposed method may not be well generalised to other code translation tasks (e.g., between different program languages).

In the main paper, all experiments are conducted on Python due to the scarcity of deep learning programs written in other programming languages. In newly added Appendix A.11, we show that ADELT is not limited to Python in an artificial setting of transpilation from PyTorch in Python 2 to Keras in Python 3.

Unfortunately, as almost all deep learning codes are written in Python, we are unable to  evaluate ADELT to transpile other programming languages such as Java and C. However, the newly added Appendix A.11 shows that ADELT can do such transpilation under the assumption that there is enough unlabeled training data available in both languages to train a joint LM and an API keyword dictionary. Also, ADELT is a method for domain-specific transpilation for deep learning codes.  ADELT is **not intend for general  source-to-source transpilation between general-purpose programming languages (e.g., transpiling arbitrary code written in C++ to Python)**, which is considered as an extremely challenging open problem (Lachaux et al. 2020, Roziere et al. 2022).


### Weakness 3

> The method comparisons are only based on the sentence-level evaluation. I am unsure of the effectiveness of this method on true settings, e.g., generating a TensorFlow/MXNet version of the Pytorch-based DL models or toolkits.

ADELT is *not* evaluated sentence by sentence. Our evaluation benchmark consists of code fragments extracted from  deep learning codes crawled from GitHub. Our benchmarks consist of real-world deep learning codes for comparing different DL frameworks (e.g. mlperf). We show two longer examples in our benchmark in the newly added Appendix A.10. To evaluate ADELT’s accuracy, we use BLEU, F1, and Exact Match as **evaluation metrics, none of which is sentence-level** : if and only if two code pieces to be exactly the same after canonicalization, they are considered as an exact match pair.

### Question 1

> What if the API keywords are not aligned well in different DL frameworks? It seems that the proposed method would fail in this situation.

We observe that most cases in the transpilation between deep learning frameworks are one-one API keyword mappings as DL frameworks follow similar designs. That said, there are indeed cases where such mappings are not one-one mappings, as we show in Section 3.6 and Appendix A.9. ADELT can also solve such cases if enough unlabeled training data is available, by adding a new API call when the match score with a new API call in the similarity matrix reaches some threshold.

### Question 2

> For the construction of the API keyword translation dictionary, do you try to leverage the technical document of API calls to directly align the API keyword in different DL frameworks? I think it is an easy way to achieve this goal.

Thank you for your interesting ideas. We did not explore that as the exact match accuracy of ADELT is already very high. We will keep that in mind as we apply our technique to other domains.

### Question 3

> Please provide some example comparisons of model modules.

We added another two examples in the newly added Appendix A.10, where two complete PyTorch classes consisting of multiple statements are transpiled to Keras correctly.

content.title: Thank you for your comments
content.comment:
Thank you for your comments. We answer the question in your comments below. We hope it addresses your concern regarding the reproducibility and generalizability of our method.

> As there is no released data and model output, I cannot well judge the performance of the proposed method (surprising improvements on EM score)

1. We have released codes, pretrained models, and training data in the supplementary material, which would be sufficient to reproduce ADELT and get all outputs of ADELT. We also included the outputs of GPT-3 and Codex for reference in the supplementary material.

1. The improvements from Codex (56.00/60.00/53.20/56.46) to ADELT (75.33/72.50/69.98/63.67) on EM score are not surprising. The programs transpiled by Codex usually have correct skeletons but are inaccurate on API-specific details, such as such as the ordering of arguments to API calls. However, the EM score is a very strict metric: a code piece is considered to be transpiled correctly if and only if both the code skeleton and all API keywords are correct. As programs transpiled by end-to-end LMs usually have the correct skeletons but are inaccurate on one or two API-specific details, such cases are scored as 0 in terms of the EM score. This is why ADELT can achieve such a large gain in EM score by mapping API keywords with higher accuracy.

> (I cannot well judge) whether this method could be generalised to more complex code translation tasks.

This paper primarily focuses on transpilation between deep learning frameworks, which is a practical, challenging, and meaningful task. In the rebuttal revision, we fully automate our method for transpiling skeletal codes: the code skeleton is transpiled using Codex by few-shot prompting. In Appendix A.11, we show how this simple change allows ADELT to be applied to transpilation tasks where the source and the target are in **different programming languages**. In Section 3.6 and Appendix A.9, we show how ADELT can solve **one-to-many** API mappings when enough unlabeled training data is available. Therefore, while we think that transpiling between deep learning frameworks is already challenging and practical enough to be presented as a standalone paper, we believe some of our techniques should be generalized to other tasks as well, such as transpilation between different SQL dialects, or even data visualization APIs.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper presents and analyzes 'Adversarial Deep Learning Transpiler' (ADELT), a system that transcripts a deep learning framework to a new source code. It can be trained in an unsupervised way (no labelled data) and uses both textual and contextual representations of the API keywords. Using domain-adversarial paradigm, ADELT trains a generator to map this vector to an aligned embedding space. A corpus for Python-Keras-MXNet compilation (three popular and largely used DL libraries) is also provided.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
STRENGTHS
- The paper considers a practical problem in the space of software and tools development, like (re)building DL frameworks that use the libraries used herein (which tend to update fast usually).

- The authors have performed extensive experiments for the validation of their system quality. Section 3 describes the setup and the evaluation comparison to existing models (table 1)

- A trait of this paper is that it uses as 'dataset' (essentially python code) the unlabeled DL corpus that authors collected from web data, without resorting to hand-crafted rules.

- By considering a language specific feature such as API keywords, the code optimizes the cost to developing the transpiler framework. This could cut down the cost of memory and time efficiency of the model significantly. 

WEAKNESSES
- When training the generator and the output embeddings, the choice of mini-batch SGD seems arbitrary or probably based on the general notion that most approaches today use this. Could it be possible that SGD is not the best suited approach in this context; could loss minimization approach be used? In the appendix the authors specify the other hyperparameters used, but are these in relation with running the underlying algorithm or related with the Python libraries used in building these transpilers?

- Accounting for a language specific feature such as API keywords seems to limit the applicability of the model. 

- Could the authors explain the motivation/the need of providing such a transpilation system?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Reproducibility: The authors provide the code, corpus and experimental setting online allowing for reproducibility. 
Novelty: The novelty of this work is towards building a code transpiler which could be considered useful for multiple use cases, such as in software development toolkits and modular code changes. To widen the scope and use of these tools the authors could consider other use cases for transpilers (not just in the context of neural machine translation), exploring other programming languages or source-target libraries or explore the optimization of memory bandwidths or runtime.
Quality: The presentation and description seems ok.
Clarity: The ideas seems clear.
content.summary_of_the_review:
It seems to be a novel work; overall an ok paper.

POST REBUTTAL: After reading carefully the reviews from the other reviewers and the new version of the paper, I have some more comments:
STRENGTHS: I think that the paper presents a novel 'pipeline' and a novel handling of the topic (end to end transpilation for deep neural network systems).
The authors pay attention to the writing and to their references, showing their effort in communicating their findings.

WEAKNESSES: About the scores which are the ones to prove the paper's superiority over similar papers/systems, it seems that the most succinct and 'reliable' metric is the Exact Match (since we are talking about code as 'output' and we are interested in the exact semantics, or better in the 'achieved task' of the produced code). Focusing on the EM scores, we observe that the given system achieves a surprising raise in the score (from 25.1 to 63.37). What is the explanation of the such a great success in the transpilation that this system introduces? Is it data driven or is there a pipeline component that particularly directs the system to producing higher matching?

Would the authors like to provide intuition (if not explanation) about this issue?

content.title: Response to Reviewer kiHn
content.comment:
Thank you for your encouraging comments. We respond to your comments below to address your concerns.

### Weakness 1

> When training the generator and the output embeddings, the choice of mini-batch SGD seems arbitrary or probably based on the general notion that most approaches today use this. Could it be possible that SGD is not the best suited approach in this context; could loss minimization approach be used? In the appendix the authors specify the other hyperparameters used, but are these in relation with running the underlying algorithm or related with the Python libraries used in building these transpilers?

SGD is the standard approach used in domain adversarial training (Ganin et al., 2016), and we use SGD following this standard practice and related work (Conneau et al., 2018).

Appendix A.2 describes the hyperparameters we used when we ran the underlying adversarial training algorithm.

### Weakness 2

> Accounting for a language specific feature such as API keywords seems to limit the applicability of the model.

Please refer to our new version of the paper. The new version of ADELT can be integrated with pretrained big LMs for skeletal code transpilation. This modification improves the flexibility of ADELT so that it can potentially be applied to a wider variety of scenarios. As an illustration, we used our updated algorithm to transpile PyTorch code in Python 2 to Keras code in Python 3, as described in Appendix A.11.

### Weakness 3

> Could the authors explain the motivation/the need of providing such a transpilation system?

1. With new deep learning frameworks appearing every year, migrating deep learning codes from one framework to another is a tedious chore even for expert DL practitioners. An automated tool will help developers overcome this difficulty.

1. The most popular solution for translation without parallel training data is zero-shot/few-shot prompting using pretrained big language models. However, in our early explorations, we find that such pretrained LMs are very inaccurate in transpiling API function names and parameter names (Codex can only get up to 67.5% accuracy in PyTorch-Keras keyword translation, where ADELT can achieve 85.42%). So a specialized algorithm is needed.

1. The task of transpiling API keywords is analogous to word translation in NLP. Inspired by related work in word translation (Conneau et al., 2018), we design our algorithm based on domain adversarial training.

1. That said, programming languages have more structural properties than natural languages that can be used in transpilation. We leverage these properties in both our preprocessing pipeline and the hierarchical dictionary generation algorithm, resulting in ADELT.

### References

- Yaroslav Ganin, Evgeniya Ustinova, Hana Ajakan, Pascal Germain, Hugo Larochelle, François Laviolette, Mario Marchand, and Victor Lempitsky. Domain-adversarial training of neural networks. arXiv:1505.07818.
- Alexis Conneau, Guillaume Lample, Marc’Aurelio Ranzato, Ludovic Denoyer, and Hervé Jégou. Word translation without parallel data. arXiv:1710.04087.

content.title: General Response to all Reviewers
content.comment:
We thank all reviewers for their helpful comments. To address the reviewer's concerns, we uploaded a new version of our paper, where we fully automate our method for transpiling skeletal codes (i.e., code that remains after all API keywords are replaced with placeholders, as discussed in Section 2.2). In our previous version of ADELT, only API keywords are substituted according to the learned API dictionary, while the code skeleton is transpiled manually via copy-and-paste. In the new version of ADELT, the code skeleton is transpiled using Codex, a pretrained big language model, by few-shot prompting. This change improves the flexibility of ADELT by fully automating our transpilation algorithm, and enabling our approach to apply to more general scenarios (different programming languages, other application domains, etc.).

In Appendix A.10, we added two examples in the evaluation benchmark as requested by reviewers. In Appendix A.11, we also describe how ADELT can be applied to transpilation tasks where the source and the target are in different programming languages.
